source_text: Commentarius in Psalmum [Sp.] (fragmenta) ̓Εκ τῆς ἑρμηνείας τοῦ ιεʹ ψαλμοῦ· Ἀλλὰ μὴν ἡ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἑκατέρων πεῖραν ἔσχε. Γέγονε γὰρ καὶ ἐν τῷ χωρίῳ τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων ψυχῶν, καὶ τῆς σαρκὸς ἐκτὸς γενομένη ζῇ καὶ ὑφέστηκε. Λογικὴ ἄρα, καὶ ταῖς ψυχαῖς τῶν ἀνθρώπων ὁμοούσιος, ὥσπερ καὶ ἡ σὰρξ ὁμοούσιος τῇ τῶν ἀνθρώπων σαρκὶ τυγχάνει, ἐκ τῆς Μαρίας προελθοῦσα. Εὐσταθίου Ἀντιοχείας ἐξ ἑρμηνείας τοῦ ιεʹ ψαλμοῦ· Ἐξαπέστειλεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός· οὐ γενομένους, ἀλλὰ γενόμενον· μοναδικὸν γὰρ τὸ πρόσωπον· οὐκ εἶπον μοναδικὴν τὴν φύσιν· ἄπαγε, μὴ γένοιτο· οὐδὲ τὴν αὐτὴν οὐσίαν σαρκὸς καὶ θεότητος, ἀλλ' εἶπον ἕνα Κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν, δι' οὗ τὰ πάντα, ἐν τῷ διαφόρῳ τῶν φύσεων, γνωριζόμενον κατὰ πάντα.
thought_title: The soul of Jesus is rational and of the same substance as human souls
orientation: Eustathius of Antioch is opening his interpretation of Psalm 15 by arguing that Jesus possessed a human soul as well as human flesh.
pass_a_gloss: From the interpretation of the fifteenth psalm: But indeed the soul of Jesus had experience of both. For it came to be also in the region of human souls, and having come to be outside the flesh it lives and subsists. Therefore it is rational, and of the same substance as the souls of human beings, just as also the flesh happens to be of the same substance as the flesh of human beings, having come forth from Mary. From Eustathius of Antioch, from the interpretation of the fifteenth psalm: God sent his Son, born of a woman; not born ones, but born one; for the person is singular; I did not say the nature is singular; far be it; nor the same substance of flesh and divinity, but I said one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, known in all things in the distinction of natures.

choices.why: πεῖραν ἔσχε means 'had experience of'; ἑκατέρων is genitive plural 'of both', referring to soul and flesh.

choices.term: ἐν τῷ χωρίῳ τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων ψυχῶν
choices.english: in the region of human souls
choices.why: χωρίον means 'place, region'; the phrase suggests the soul of Jesus entered the realm or condition of human souls.
rejected: in the place of human souls
in the territory of human souls

choices.english: having come to be outside the flesh
choices.why: ἐκτός with genitive means 'outside of'; γενομένη is aorist middle participle of γίνομαι, 'having come to be'.
rejected: having become apart from the flesh

choices.why: ζῇ is present indicative 'lives'; ὑφέστηκε is perfect indicative of ὑφίστημι, 'subsists, has real existence'.

choices.english: away with it, may it not be
choices.why: ἄπαγε is an interjection of rejection, 'away with it!'; μὴ γένοιτο is the standard optative of denial, 'may it not be!'.
rejected: far be it, let it not happen

choices.why: διάφορος means 'different, distinct'; the dative with ἐν expresses the sphere in which Christ is known.

pass_b_english: But surely the soul of Jesus had experience of both. For it came to be in the region of human souls, and having come to be outside the flesh it lives and subsists. It is therefore rational and of the same substance as the souls of human beings, just as his flesh is of the same substance as human flesh, having come forth from Mary.

From the interpretation of Psalm 15 by Eustathius of Antioch: “God sent his Son, born of a woman” (Galatians 4:4). He did not say “born ones,” but “born”—for the person is singular. I did not say the nature is singular; away with it, may it not be! Nor did I say that flesh and divinity have the same substance. But I said one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things exist, known in every way in the distinction of natures.

last_rejected.quote: I did not say the nature is singular; away with it, may it not be! Nor did I say that flesh and divinity have the same substance. But I said one Lord Jesus Christ
last_rejected.source_quote: οὐκ εἶπον μοναδικὴν τὴν φύσιν· ἄπαγε, μὴ γένοιτο· οὐδὲ τὴν αὐτὴν οὐσίαν σαρκὸς καὶ θεότητος, ἀλλ' εἶπον ἕνα Κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν
last_rejected.why: Greek uses 1st person singular (εἶπον, εἶπον) but English 'I' makes Eustathius the speaker; context shows he's quoting/paraphrasing the apostolic formula's intended meaning, not his own words. The Greek is ambiguous but the 'I' is likely the biblical speaker or a rhetorical 'we'. The English 'I' is misleading.
last_rejected.fix: It does not say 'the nature is singular'—away with it, may it never be! Nor does it say that flesh and divinity have the same substance. But it says 'one Lord Jesus Christ'
last_rejected.ruling: εἶπον is 1st person singular; Eustathius is the speaker throughout. 'I' correctly renders it. No ambiguity or misattribution.
